cake-or-cupcake-white-with-white-icing-b.title: Cake or cupcake, white with white icing

content.title: About
content.content: A cake or cupcake with white icing is a baked treat made from a soft batter, usually consisting of wheat flour, eggs, sugar, and butter, topped with a smooth white frosting made from powdered sugar and cream. This dessert is popular in bakeries and is often served at celebrations, weddings, and special events.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: White icing is traditionally prepared from powdered sugar, butter, and a small amount of milk or cream to achieve a silky texture.
Cupcakes are often decorated not only with icing but also with edible glitter, nuts, or berries for contrast.
The classic sponge layer in a cake can be brushed with syrup to keep it moist and flavorful.
In some countries cupcakes are served with tea, while in the US they are commonly sold as individual portions called "cupcakes".
The white color of the dessert symbolizes purity and is frequently used for wedding cakes.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Cake or cupcake provides carbohydrates that quickly supply the body with energy.

items.title: Contains protein
items.content: Eggs and dairy ingredients supply a modest amount of protein needed for tissue repair.

items.title: Calcium from dairy
items.content: Butter and milk in the frosting and batter contribute to bone health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Flour and eggs are sources of B1, B2, and B6 vitamins, which support metabolism.

items.title: Antioxidants in cream
items.content: Cream may contain small amounts of vitamin E, an antioxidant that protects cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Large amounts of sugar can contribute to weight gain and increase the risk of tooth decay.

items.title: Gluten and dairy allergies
items.content: The batter contains wheat flour and the icing contains dairy, which may trigger reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Calorie dense
items.content: Cakes and cupcakes are calorie‑rich, so they should be enjoyed in moderation, especially on weight‑control diets.

items.title: Potential trans fats
items.content: If the recipe uses margarine, trans fats may be present, which are unfavorable for heart health.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the cake or cupcake as a standalone dessert, paired with berry sauce, ice cream, or fresh fruit. Bite‑size cupcakes are easy to eat by hand, while larger cakes are typically sliced and enjoyed with a cup of coffee or tea.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the finished cake or cupcakes in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 2 days. For longer storage, refrigerate them – they stay fresh for up to 5 days. Before serving, allow the dessert to come to room temperature so the icing softens.

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken nuggets are breaded pieces of chicken breast meat that are deep‑fried or baked. They are a common item in school cafeterias as a quick, portable source of protein. Inside they contain tender meat, while the outside is a crispy golden crust.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first commercial nugget recipe was created in the United States in the 1970s.
In school menus nuggets are often served with barbecue, sweet chili, or ketchup sauces.
To reduce fat content, many cafeterias bake nuggets instead of deep‑frying them.
Nuggets can be made from various parts of the chicken, but most commonly use breast meat.
Some countries have introduced portion‑size limits for nuggets in schools to control calorie intake.

items.title: Protein source
items.content: Chicken meat is rich in complete protein, essential for growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Contains vitamin B6
items.content: Vitamin B6 supports amino‑acid metabolism and nervous‑system function.

items.title: Iron source
items.content: Iron from chicken helps maintain hemoglobin levels and prevents anemia.

items.title: Provides zinc
items.content: Zinc is important for immune function and wound healing.

items.title: Contains phosphorus
items.content: Phosphorus is necessary for healthy bones and teeth.

items.title: High fat and calorie content
items.content: Fried nuggets can be calorie‑dense and contain saturated fats, which are undesirable when eaten frequently.

items.title: Sodium
items.content: Salt used in the breading can increase sodium intake, which may affect blood pressure.

items.title: Chicken allergy
items.content: A small number of people may be allergic to chicken proteins.

items.title: Trans fats in breading
items.content: Some pre‑made breadings contain partially hydrogenated oils, a source of trans fats.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Nuggets are typically served hot and are easy to eat with your hands. Pair them with vegetable sticks, mashed potatoes, or whole‑grain bread. For a healthier option, choose baked nuggets and limit sugary dipping sauces.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked nuggets in the refrigerator for up to 2–3 days. Frozen nuggets keep for up to 3 months at –18 °C. Reheat thoroughly until the internal temperature reaches 75 °C.

egg-omelet-or-scrambled-egg-made-with-oi.title: Egg omelet or scrambled egg, made with oil

content.title: About
content.content: Omelets and scrambled eggs are dishes made from eggs cooked in vegetable oil. Eggs provide high‑quality protein, B‑group vitamins, vitamin D, and minerals such as iron and selenium. Cooking in oil adds energy and fat‑soluble vitamins but also raises the calorie count.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Eggs were first domesticated more than 6,000 years ago in Southeast Asia.
Frying in oil creates a golden crust that locks moisture inside the dish.
Different oils (sunflower, olive, butter) give distinct flavors and aromas.
Eggs are often used as a binding agent in cooking, replacing flour or starch.
In 1973 the United States mandated mandatory labeling of cholesterol content in foods, including eggs.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Eggs contain all essential amino acids, making them a complete protein for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Eggs are high in vitamins B2, B6, and B12, which support energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Fat‑soluble vitamins
items.content: Oil helps absorb vitamins A, D, E, and K present in the yolk.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Eggs provide iron, zinc, and selenium, important for immunity and antioxidant protection.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: Egg‑based dishes fit well into low‑carb dietary patterns.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Some individuals may develop allergic reactions ranging from skin rashes to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Cholesterol
items.content: The yolk contains cholesterol; people with high cholesterol should consume eggs in moderation.

items.title: Calorie density
items.content: Cooking with oil increases the dish’s energy content, which can contribute to weight gain if over‑consumed.

items.title: Trans fats in oil
items.content: Highly refined oils may contain small amounts of trans fats.

content.title: How to Cook
content.content: Beat the eggs with a pinch of salt and pepper. Heat a skillet, add 1‑2 tsp of vegetable oil, pour in the egg mixture and cook over medium heat, stirring for scrambled eggs or leaving untouched until set for an omelet.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh eggs in the refrigerator at 1‑4 °C for up to 3‑4 weeks. Cooked omelets or scrambled eggs can be kept in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 2 days, reheating before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Empanada, beef, with vegetables is a traditional Spanish‑Latin American pastry made from thin dough filled with seasoned ground beef, carrots, sweet pepper and onion. The dough is usually fried until golden, giving a crisp exterior and a juicy interior.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The word empanada comes from “empanar,” meaning “to wrap in dough.”
In different countries the filling may include cheese, chicken, seafood or even sweet fruit.
Empanadas are traditionally served at holidays and family celebrations, especially in Argentina and Chile.
The dough often contains wheat flour, butter and a small amount of yeast, which makes it light and airy.
One theory says empanadas were first made in Spain during colonization and later adapted in South America.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Ground beef provides high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Beef and vegetables supply B12, niacin and riboflavin, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Iron
items.content: Beef is a good source of heme iron, which is readily absorbed by the body.

items.title: Fiber from vegetables
items.content: Carrots and sweet pepper add dietary fiber that promotes healthy digestion.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Vegetables contain beta‑carotene and vitamin C, helping combat free radicals.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: Using fatty ground beef or deep‑frying the pastry can make the dish calorie‑dense.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: The wheat‑based dough contains gluten, which may trigger reactions in people with celiac disease.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: Added salt in the filling can increase sodium intake, which is a concern for hypertension.

items.title: Potential pathogens
items.content: Beef must be cooked thoroughly to avoid risks of salmonella or other food‑borne infections.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Empanadas are served hot as a snack or main dish, accompanied by salsa, sour cream or guacamole. They are easy to eat with hands, breaking them into bite‑size pieces.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked empanadas in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. For longer storage, freeze them in a bag for up to 2 months and reheat in the oven until crisp.

content.title: About
content.content: Monster is a popular energy drink containing caffeine, taurine, B‑vitamins and sugar (or sugar substitutes). It is sold in various flavors and sizes, including a 550 ml can. The drink is intended to boost alertness and concentration.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first Monster drink was launched in 2002 by Monster Beverage Corporation.
The brand is known for its bold can design with the iconic “M” logo and aggressive marketing in extreme sports.
A typical 500 ml can contains about 160 mg of caffeine, roughly equivalent to two cups of coffee.
There are more than 30 flavors, including the original “Original”, sugar‑free “Zero Ultra”, and tropical “Pipeline Punch”.
Monster sponsors numerous music festivals, esports teams and athletes.

items.title: Energy boost
items.content: Caffeine stimulates the central nervous system, temporarily increasing alertness and reducing perceived fatigue.

items.title: Improved focus
items.content: B‑vitamins (B2, B3, B6, B12) support energy metabolism and may help maintain cognitive performance.

items.title: Recovery aid
items.content: Taurine and electrolytes (sodium, potassium) help maintain fluid balance during intense physical activity.

items.title: Excessive caffeine intake
items.content: High caffeine doses can cause anxiety, insomnia, rapid heartbeat and increased blood pressure.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Regular versions contain up to 55 g of sugar per 500 ml, which may contribute to weight gain and dental caries.

items.title: Interaction with alcohol
items.content: Mixing energy drinks with alcohol can mask intoxication, raising the risk of overexertion.

items.title: Not recommended for children and pregnant women
items.content: Due to high caffeine and stimulant levels, the product is not advised for people under 18, pregnant or nursing women.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Drink Monster chilled, straight from the can. A typical serving is 250–500 ml over 2–3 hours. Do not exceed 2–3 cans per day, especially if you are caffeine‑sensitive.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, consume within 24 hours for best taste.

content.title: About
content.content: Greek Salad, no dressing is a classic Mediterranean mix of fresh vegetables: tomatoes, cucumbers, sweet bell pepper, red onion, Kalamata olives, and feta cheese. The ingredients are cut into generous pieces and served without any added sauce, letting the natural flavors shine.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The salad originated on the island of Crete in the early 20th century.
Kalamata olives are one of the oldest cultivated olive varieties in Greece.
Traditional feta is made from sheep's milk, sometimes blended with goat's milk.
The original recipe does not include olive oil; it is added only at the table if desired.
Greek salad is often served as a meze (appetizer) alongside bread or pita.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Tomatoes and olives provide lycopene and polyphenols that help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports cardiovascular health
items.content: Olives contain monounsaturated fats that can help lower LDL cholesterol.

items.title: Source of vitamin K
items.content: Bell pepper and leafy greens are high in vitamin K, important for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Bone support
items.content: Feta cheese supplies calcium and phosphorus, essential for strong bones.

items.title: Hydration and cellular nutrition
items.content: Cucumbers are about 95 % water and provide electrolytes.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Feta may trigger reactions in people with lactose intolerance or milk allergy.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Feta and olives are often brined; those monitoring salt intake should limit portions.

items.title: Foodborne illness
items.content: If vegetables are not washed thoroughly, they can harbor bacteria that cause food poisoning.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the salad in a large bowl, allowing each person to take a portion. It can be enjoyed on its own, with whole‑grain bread or pita, or as part of a mezze platter.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared salad in an airtight container in the refrigerator for no more than 24 hours to maintain crispness. Store feta separately in a small container with a bit of brine.

pasta-whole-grain-with-tomato-based-sauc.title: Whole Grain Pasta with Tomato Sauce and Meat, Ready-to-Heat

content.title: About
content.content: Whole grain pasta with tomato sauce and meat pieces is a ready‑to‑heat meal that can be quickly warmed in a microwave or on the stove. It contains whole‑grain pasta, a tomato‑based sauce, tender meat (usually beef or pork), and a blend of spices. Designed for a convenient, nutritious lunch or dinner.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Whole grain pasta provides more fiber and micronutrients than traditional white‑flour pasta.
The tomato sauce is rich in lycopene, a powerful antioxidant that supports heart health.
Meat adds a complete set of essential amino acids.
The dish is formulated for fast preparation: only 2–3 minutes in the microwave are needed.
Herbs such as basil and oregano are often included, enhancing flavor without extra salt.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Whole grain pasta supplies dietary fiber, promoting healthy digestion and satiety.

items.title: Good source of protein
items.content: The meat component provides high‑quality protein essential for tissue repair and muscle maintenance.

items.title: Lycopene and antioxidants
items.content: Tomatoes deliver lycopene, which helps protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The meal contains B1, B3, and B6 vitamins that support energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Iron, zinc, and magnesium are present, contributing to immune function and nerve health.

items.title: Gluten sensitivity
items.content: Whole grain pasta contains gluten, making the product unsuitable for people with celiac disease or gluten intolerance.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: The tomato sauce can be salty; individuals monitoring sodium intake should consider the total daily amount.

items.title: Meat fat
items.content: Depending on the meat type, the dish may contain saturated fats; moderation is advised.

items.title: Heat hotspots
items.content: Microwave heating may create hot spots; stir the meal before serving to ensure even temperature.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the portion in the microwave (about 2–3 minutes) or on the stovetop, stir, let it cool slightly, and serve. Optional additions include fresh herbs, grated cheese, or a drizzle of olive oil for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the unopened package in a cool, dry place. Once opened, keep the product refrigerated and consume within 3–4 days. Discard if you notice off‑odors or discoloration.

potato-boiled-from-fresh-peel-not-eaten-.title: Boiled Potato, fresh, peel not eaten, with margarine

content.title: About
content.content: Boiled potato made from fresh tubers is a dish of cooked potatoes that have been peeled and seasoned with margarine. It has a soft, tender texture and a mild buttery flavor, making it a versatile base for many meals.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Boiled potatoes retain most of their vitamin C, which degrades during long storage of raw tubers.
Margarine used in the preparation is often fortified with vitamins A and D.
Potato is one of the world’s most consumed vegetables, with over 350 million tonnes produced annually.
Peeling before boiling reduces fiber content but makes the product easier to digest.
In some cultures boiled potatoes are served with margarine instead of butter to lower saturated fat intake.

items.title: Rich source of potassium
items.content: Potatoes provide a high amount of potassium, which supports normal blood pressure and muscle function.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Boiled potatoes contain vitamins B6 and B9, important for metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Energy supply
items.content: Starch‑based carbohydrates give a quick source of energy.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Without added margarine, potatoes contain almost no fat, making them suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Digestive support
items.content: Easily digestible starch aids normal digestion, especially for children and the elderly.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Boiled potatoes can raise blood sugar quickly, which may be undesirable for people with diabetes.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: When adding salt to margarine, monitor the amount to avoid excessive sodium intake.

items.title: Margarine allergy
items.content: Some individuals may react to the plant oils used in margarine.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Boiled potatoes with margarine can be served as a side dish, added to salads, baked under a cheese crust, or incorporated into soups. For extra flavor, sprinkle fresh herbs or spices.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store boiled potatoes in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Reheat to an internal temperature of at least 75 °C before eating. Do not keep at room temperature for more than 2 hours to prevent bacterial growth.

potato-salad-with-egg-made-with-italian-.title: Potato Salad with Egg, Made with Italian Dressing

content.title: About
content.content: A salad of boiled potatoes, hard‑boiled eggs and vegetables, tossed with an Italian dressing (olive oil, vinegar, mustard, herbs). It is a light dish popular in summer and at picnics.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The Italian dressing gives the salad a distinctive aroma of basil, oregano and garlic.
In warm weather many Russians replace the traditional “Olivier” with this lighter potato‑egg salad.
Eggs add an extra source of protein, making the dish more filling.
Potatoes retain a good amount of vitamin C when not overcooked.
The salad can be prepared ahead, but add the dressing just before serving to avoid soggy potatoes.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Eggs and potatoes provide vitamin B6 and B12, which support energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Source of healthy fats
items.content: Olive oil in the Italian dressing is high in monounsaturated fats that are heart‑friendly.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Potato skins and added vegetables (e.g., green onions) contribute fiber for better digestion.

items.title: Promotes satiety
items.content: The combination of carbohydrates (potato) and protein (egg) helps keep you feeling full longer.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Herbs such as basil and oregano contain polyphenols that combat free radicals.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to eggs, ranging from skin rashes to anaphylaxis.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: If salt is added to the dressing, the dish can become too salty, which is undesirable for hypertension.

items.title: Bacterial contamination risk
items.content: Eggs must be fully cooked and the finished salad stored in the refrigerator for no more than 2‑3 days.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Olive oil increases the calorie count; portion control is advised for weight‑management diets.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the salad chilled as a side dish or a light main course. It can be eaten with a fork or spoon, or used as a filling for sandwiches.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the salad in an airtight container in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C. Stir before serving to redistribute the dressing. Discard if it develops an off‑odor or discoloration.

content.title: About
content.content: Refried beans are a smooth puree made from cooked beans that are fried with a small amount of oil, spices, and salt. They are a staple in Mexican‑style fast‑food restaurants, often served as a side for tacos, burritos, nachos, and other dishes. The texture is creamy, the flavor slightly smoky and mildly seasoned.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Traditionally refried beans are made from black or pinto beans, but in the U.S. red beans are also common.
The name “refried” comes from the Spanish “frijoles refritos,” where the prefix “re‑” means “well‑cooked,” not “fried again.”
In Mexico beans are a basic food, and refried beans are often served as a standalone dish.
Some restaurants add cheese, onions, or chili to boost flavor.
Refried beans are frequently used in vegetarian and vegan meals as a protein source.

items.title: Rich source of plant protein
items.content: Beans provide about 8 g of protein per 100 g, helping maintain muscle mass.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Contains iron and folate
items.content: These micronutrients are important for blood formation and nervous‑system health.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Beans raise blood sugar slowly, which is beneficial for people with diabetes.

items.title: Beneficial plant fats
items.content: The small amount of oil used provides essential fatty acids.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to beans.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Prepared versions often contain a lot of salt; low‑sodium options are recommended for those with hypertension.

items.title: Gas and bloating
items.content: Beans can cause gastrointestinal discomfort in sensitive people.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Because of added oil, refried beans are more calorie‑dense than plain boiled beans.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve refried beans hot as a side, use as a filling for tacos, burritos, chimichangas, or as a dip for nachos. They can be mixed into salads, soups, or incorporated into vegetarian patties.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep refried beans in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 5 days. For longer storage, freeze in portions for up to 3 months. Reheat to at least 75 °C before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Vegetable soup with meat is a hot dish that combines fresh vegetables with tender meat. It is rich in vitamins, minerals, and protein, making it a nutritious and satisfying option for lunch or dinner.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Traditionally this soup is prepared in many world cuisines, using local vegetables and spices.
Meat soups help keep the body warm in cold weather.
Vegetables retain most of their nutrients thanks to the short cooking time.
Any type of meat can be used: beef, pork, chicken, or turkey.
Homemade bone broth gives the soup a richer flavor and adds extra collagen.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Meat and vegetables provide B1, B2, B6, and B12 vitamins, which support energy metabolism and the nervous system.

items.title: Source of protein
items.content: Meat supplies high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Contains fiber
items.content: Vegetables add dietary fiber, promoting healthy digestion and satiety.

items.title: Minerals for bones
items.content: The broth and vegetables are good sources of calcium, magnesium, and phosphorus, important for bone health.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: A warm broth helps maintain the body's fluid balance.

items.title: Meat allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to certain types of meat and should exercise caution.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Using ready‑made broth or adding salt can make the soup too salty, which is undesirable for hypertension.

items.title: Bacterial contamination
items.content: Undercooked meat may contain harmful bacteria; ensure the soup is cooked thoroughly.

items.title: Digestive issues
items.content: Large amounts of fatty meat can cause heaviness in people with sensitive digestion.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the soup hot, often accompanied by bread, croutons, or fresh herbs. You can add sour cream, grated cheese, or spices to taste.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool the soup to room temperature, then store it in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. When frozen, it keeps for up to 2 months; thaw in the refrigerator before reheating.

content.title: About
content.content: Soybean oil is a vegetable oil extracted from the seeds of the soybean plant (Glycine max). It has a light color and a neutral flavor and is one of the most widely consumed vegetable oils in the world. It is used for frying, baking, salad dressings, margarine, and many processed foods, and is often labeled simply as vegetable oil.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Soybeans have been cultivated in East Asia for thousands of years.
Soybean oil is made by pressing or solvent-extracting the oil from soybeans and is usually refined.
It contains both omega-6 (linoleic acid) and omega-3 (alpha-linolenic acid) fatty acids.
Soybean oil is commonly used in packaged foods, sauces, and dressings.
Products labeled "vegetable oil" often contain soybean oil.

items.title: Rich in unsaturated fats
items.content: Replacing saturated fats with unsaturated fats such as those in soybean oil may support heart health.

items.title: Contains omega-3 ALA
items.content: Soybean oil provides alpha-linolenic acid, a plant-based omega-3 fatty acid.

items.title: Source of vitamin E and vitamin K
items.content: Soybean oil contains vitamin E, which acts as an antioxidant, and vitamin K, which supports normal blood clotting.

items.title: Versatile cooking oil
items.content: Its neutral flavor and fairly high smoke point suit many cooking methods.

items.title: Widely available
items.content: It is affordable and easy to find.

items.title: Soy allergy
items.content: Highly refined soybean oil usually contains little soy protein, but people with soy allergy should ask their doctor whether it is suitable for them.

items.title: High in calories
items.content: Like all oils, soybean oil is calorie-dense, so portions should be moderate.

items.title: Trans fats in hydrogenated products
items.content: Partially hydrogenated soybean oil can contain trans fats, so check labels on processed foods.

items.title: Possible medication interactions
items.content: Soybean oil contains vitamin K. People taking blood thinners should consult a healthcare professional about keeping their intake consistent.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Soybean oil can be used for frying, sautéing, baking, and roasting, as well as in salad dressings and marinades. Use it in moderation and avoid heating it until it smokes or reusing it many times.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store soybean oil in a tightly closed container in a cool, dark place away from heat and light. Once opened, use it within a few months. Discard oil that smells rancid, bitter, or like paint.
